summary: Deprecates the NAT-MIB module defined in RFC 4008 because of deficiencies found in it. All its objects are kept unchanged except that their status becomes deprecated. A companion document defines a replacement, NATV2-MIB, and this document obsoletes RFC 4008.

eli5.summary: An old form is marked 'do not use anymore' but is not thrown away, because a better form has been made.

subtitle: The NAT management MIB from RFC 4008 is retired: every object stays, but is marked deprecated.

tldr.problem: NAT-MIB, defined in RFC 4008, turned out to be a poor fit for real NAT devices. Implementations differ so much that few could claim even basic compliance.
tldr.mechanism: This memo republishes every NAT-MIB object unchanged except that its STATUS becomes deprecated. New work is pointed to a second version, NATV2-MIB, defined in RFC 7659.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7658 obsoletes RFC 4008. New implementations are encouraged to use NATV2-MIB instead.

today: RFC 7658 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 4008, and it has not itself been obsoleted or updated. It points new implementations to NATV2-MIB in RFC 7659.

sections.title: What the Memo Does
sections.content:
RFC 7658 deprecates a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB), the module called NAT-MIB, which describes devices that perform the Network Address Translator (NAT) function. New implementations are encouraged to base themselves on the second version, NATV2-MIB, defined in RFC 7659.

The abstract states the rule plainly: all MIB objects specified in RFC 4008 are included in this version unchanged, with only the STATUS changed to deprecated. This document obsoletes RFC 4008.

The memo also draws a limit around both modules. Neither NAT-MIB nor NATV2-MIB addresses firewall functions, and neither can be used for configuring or monitoring them.
sections.eli5: The old rulebook for talking to address-swapping boxes is retired, but its pages are kept as they were. Only a big 'old version' sticker is added.

sections.title: The Management Framework Behind It
sections.content:
MIB objects live in a virtual information store and are generally accessed through the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP). Objects in the MIB are defined using the Structure of Management Information (SMI).

This memo specifies a module that is compliant with SMIv2, which is described in STD 58 (RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580). For a wider overview of the Internet-Standard Management Framework, the text points readers to section 7 of RFC 3410.
sections.eli5: Think of a MIB as a list of dials and gauges on a machine, and SNMP as the way you read them from far away. The SMI is the style guide for how each dial is described.

sections.title: Why NAT-MIB Was Deprecated
sections.content:
Section 3.1 lists the reasons all objects in RFC 4008 were marked deprecated. Each comes with a lesson learned.

  • Writability: NAT implementations vary tremendously, so configuration parameters were wildly incompatible and few implementations could claim full compliance. Lesson: the MIB should be read-only as much as possible.
  • Exposing configuration parameters: even in read-only mode, many parameters (for example timeouts) were exposed. Lesson: the purpose of the MIB is not to expose configuration parameters.
  • Interfaces: the objects tied NAT state to interfaces, but many NAT implementations never track the interface or associate a mapping with a set of interfaces. Lesson: NAT is a logical function that may be independent of interfaces.
  • NAT service types: RFC 4008 used four categories (basicNat, napt, bidirectionalNat, twiceNat), which are ill-defined. Lesson: do not try to categorize NAT types.
  • Limited transport protocol set: only other, icmp, udp and tcp were defined, with numeric values unrelated to the standard protocol numbers, so DCCP, SCTP and others could not be exposed. Lesson: use standard transport protocol numbers.

Section 3.2 adds that a number of desirable new features are missing from NAT-MIB, and refers to the latter part of Section 2 of RFC 7659.
sections.eli5: The old form asked for things most machines could not fill in, and it only had room for four kinds of mail. The new one asks for less and has room for every kind.

sections.title: The Deprecated Module Definition
sections.content:
Section 4 contains the complete NAT-MIB module in SMIv2 notation, which makes up most of the 62 pages. It imports definitions from several other RFCs and refers to others, including RFC 792, RFC 4443 and RFC 3413.

The module identity, natMIB, sits at { mib-2 123 }. Its revision history records the 2 October 2015 revision as 'Deprecation of all objects, published as RFC 7658', with a pointer to NATV2-MIB in RFC 7659 as the recommended replacement. The earlier revision, dated 21 March 2005, is the initial version published as RFC 4008.

Individual definitions carry the same marker. For example, the NatProtocolType textual convention has STATUS deprecated and its description ends with 'Deprecated in favor of NATV2-MIB'.
sections.eli5: Most of the pages are the old form copied out in full, one line at a time, with the 'old version' sticker on each line.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because all objects in the module are deprecated, the security considerations in RFC 7659 apply instead. Those considerations cover the case where both this module and NATV2-MIB are present.

The text adds that such a situation is unlikely, because RFC 4008, as a MIB module oriented toward configuration, was overtaken by events and saw little implementation.
sections.eli5: The safety rules for the new form also cover the old one, and the authors think hardly anyone used the old form anyway.

sections.title: IANA Actions
sections.content:
IANA assigned object identifier 123 to the natMIB module, under the prefix iso.org.dod.internet.mgmt.mib-2, in the Network Management Parameters registry.

IANA has marked that identifier as DEPRECATED and updated the reference from RFC 4008 to this document.
sections.eli5: The official number list keeps the old entry but now says it is retired and points to this memo.
